content: Negative feedback occurs when a portion of a system's output is inverted and fed back into the system's input. This mechanism typically results in the attenuation of fluctuations within the system. Many real-world systems have specific points, often referred to as equilibrium points, around which the system tends to stabilize. When a disturbance or perturbation occurs, a system governed by negative feedback will work to restore equilibrium at these points. In physical and biological systems, opposing influences often interact to maintain balance. For instance, in biochemistry, one group of chemicals may drive a process in one direction, while another group of chemicals counteracts this by driving the process in the opposite direction. If one or both of these opposing forces exhibit non-linear behavior, the system can achieve a stable equilibrium point. In biological contexts, this regulatory process, which is often biochemical in nature, is commonly referred to as homeostasis. Biological Examples Certain biological systems rely on negative feedback mechanisms to maintain stability. Numerous physiological processes in the human body utilize negative feedback to maintain homeostasis. Examples include the regulation of body temperature and the control of blood glucose levels. When negative feedback mechanisms are disrupted, the consequences can be detrimental. For instance, if the negative feedback system responsible for regulating blood glucose levels fails, blood glucose may rise uncontrollably, potentially leading to diabetes. Social Sciences In the context of social sciences, a meta-analysis examining the delivery of negative feedback found that its impact on motivation can vary depending on how it is delivered. Negative feedback was observed to be less demotivating when the feedback included specific instructional details on how to improve, when it was based on criterion-referenced standards, and when it was delivered in person.
